1.1.title: Thinking Like a Physicist
1.1.source_note: The declared section preserves the usable Chapter 1 source and explicitly ends at a source gap. The build condenses the available source, then uses a minimal Framework bridge to complete the current vocabulary distinctions without inventing missing textbook prose.
1.1.learning_target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

i_cans.text: I can distinguish between an observation, inference, hypothesis, law, and theory.
I can explain why a claim must be testable to be scientific.
I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.

1.2.title: Forces and Newton’s First Law
1.2.source_note: The declared textbook section contains the usable 2.3 and 2.6 source passages and seven instructional source figures.
1.2.learning_target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

i_cans.text: I can state Newton’s First Law in everyday language.
I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.
I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.

1.3.title: Net Force and Vectors
1.3.source_note: The declared textbook section contains the usable 2.4 source passage and five instructional source figures; omitted source figures with no captured image are not recreated.
1.3.learning_target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.

i_cans.text: I can explain why force is a vector quantity.
I can combine forces acting in the same direction or opposite directions.
I can identify the resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare force strength and direction.

1.4.title: Equilibrium and Balanced Motion
1.4.source_note: The declared source explicitly says subsection 2.7 was unavailable. The build preserves the available 2.5 equilibrium source and uses a minimal Framework bridge for static versus dynamic equilibrium and constant-velocity language.
1.4.learning_target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

i_cans.text: I can recognize static equilibrium and dynamic equilibrium.
I can explain why an object at rest can still have forces acting on it.
I can explain why an object moving at constant speed in a straight line can be in equilibrium and use the equilibrium rule to reason about upward/downward and left/right forces.

1.5.title: Modeling Forces in the Real World
1.5.source_note: The declared textbook section explicitly identifies itself as a synthesis/application section with no corresponding textbook passage. The build therefore uses the Framework targets and the declared synthesis text, with no invented source figures.
1.5.learning_target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

i_cans.text: I can draw a force diagram for an object in a real-world situation.
I can decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.
I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.
